Guided Inquiry

1 · Look at a monatomic gas

A single atom — argon, neon, helium — can only move along x, y and z. That is three places it can store energy. Equipartition gives each one (1/2)kT per molecule, so the energy bar has three equal blocks.

Read the chain beside the atom: f → Cv → Cp → γ. Each number follows from the one before it.

2 · Predict — switch to diatomic

You are about to replace the atom with a dumbbell (like N₂, O₂, H₂). What will γ do?

3 · Observe the switch

Click the Diatomic button in the sidebar. A pink ROTATION tile appears — the dumbbell spins about two axes, one at a time — and the energy bar grows by two equal blocks — exactly equal, because that is what equipartition means.

Read the chain: f = 5, Cv = (5/2)R ≈ 20.79, Cp = Cv + R ≈ 29.10, γ = 7/5 = 1.4.

4 · Now polyatomic

Switch to Polyatomic. A third rotation axis lights up (a non-linear molecule like H₂O or CH₄ can tumble about all three body axes). f becomes 6 and γ drops to 4/3 ≈ 1.333.

The pattern is inescapable: γ = 1 + 2/f. More places to hide energy → smaller γ.

5 · Try temperature

Drag the temperature slider. Watch what moves and what does NOT. The internal energy U = nCvT changes; f, Cv, Cp and γ do not.

This is the whole idea: γ is a structural property of the molecule, not a thermal one.

01

At a glance

The sim shows one gas molecule, the separate ways it can move and spin, and a chain of numbers that turns that count into heat capacities and γ. You swap the molecule and the numbers follow.

What you'll learn

  • How the number of ways a molecule can store energy, its degrees of freedom f, is counted.
  • How f fixes the molar heat capacities CV and CP and the ratio γ = CP/CV.
  • How temperature enters the internal energy U of the gas.

  • Internal energy panel (sidebar): U for one mole.

03

Each quadratic mode stores ½ kT

Equipartition says that at temperature T, every independent way a molecule can store energy as a squared term, such as ½mv² for a motion or ½Iω² for a spin, holds ½ kT on average per molecule. The number of such terms is the degrees of freedom, f.

An atom of argon, neon or helium is a point-like mass. It can move along x, y and z, and it has nothing to spin or stretch, so f = 3. The average energy per atom is 3 × ½ kT = (3/2) kT. For one mole, with R = NAk:

U = (3/2)RT · CV = (3/2)R = 12.47 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
U = 3742 J at 300 K for one mole, which is the sim's opening reading.
See itLook at the energy share bar for the monatomic molecule. Watch for: three lit blocks, the label U/molecule ≈ 1.5 kT, and the internal energy panel reading 3742 J.
04

A diatomic molecule counts five modes

A dumbbell such as N₂, O₂ or H₂ can still move along x, y and z, which gives 3 modes. It can also tumble end over end about two axes at right angles to the bond, which gives 2 more. That makes f = 5, and 5 × ½ kT = (5/2) kT per molecule.

  • Spinning about the bond itself stores nothing, because the atoms are point-like on that axis and have almost no moment of inertia about it.
  • The bond could also vibrate like a spring, which would add 2 more terms (kinetic and potential). For N₂ and O₂ that needs temperatures well above 1000 K, so in this range the vibration stays frozen and counts 0. The sim shows it as a grey tile marked frozen.
See itSwitch the molecule from monatomic to diatomic. Watch for: a pink rotation tile appearing, the dumbbell spinning about one axis at a time, and five lit blocks in the energy bar.
05

A non-linear polyatomic molecule counts six modes

A bent or three-dimensional molecule such as H₂O or CH₄ has atoms spread through space, so it has a real moment of inertia about all three body axes. It tumbles about each of them.

  • Translation: 3 modes.
  • Rotation: 3 modes, one more than the dumbbell.
  • Vibration: frozen over the sim's temperature range, as before.

So f = 6, and the energy per molecule is 6 × ½ kT = 3 kT. A linear molecule such as CO₂ spins about two axes only, so the sim's polyatomic case does not describe it.

See itSwitch the molecule to polyatomic. Watch for: the rotation tile running through three axes in turn, and all six blocks lit.
06

The chain from f to γ

The mole's energy is U = (f/2)RT, so CV = (f/2)R. At constant pressure the gas also does work p dV, which for one mole costs an extra R for each kelvin (Mayer's relation), so CP = CV + R. Then

γ = CP/CV = (f + 2)/f = 1 + 2/f
fCV (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)CPγ
312.4720.791.667
520.7929.101.400
624.9433.261.333

CP − CV stays R however many modes there are, so more modes make the ratio smaller. Mass, size and the name of the gas never enter.

See itRead the four chain cards for the diatomic molecule. Watch for: f = 5, CV = 20.79, CP = 29.10 and γ = 1.400.
07

Temperature changes U, not the mode count

U = nCVT grows in proportion to T. For one mole of the diatomic gas it rises from 2079 J at 100 K to 20786 J at 1000 K, while f, CV, CP and γ keep their values on the chain.

The mode count is a property of the molecule's structure, so a temperature change alone does not alter it. The sim holds f fixed from 100 K to 1000 K.

Real gases do change f where a mode switches on or off. Vibration begins to count at a few thousand kelvin for N₂ and O₂, which would raise f to 7 and lower γ to 1.286. Hydrogen's rotation freezes out below about 100 K, and its heat capacity then falls toward the monatomic value. Equipartition cannot predict this, because it is a quantum effect.

See itTake the diatomic gas to 900 K. Watch for: the internal energy panel reading 18708 J while the four chain cards keep their values.
08

Where it matters

  • Adiabatic compression. For a reversible adiabatic change, TVγ−1 is constant. Halving the volume raises T by a factor of 22/3 = 1.59 for a monatomic gas and 20.4 = 1.32 for a diatomic one.
  • Speed of sound. Sound in an ideal gas travels at √(γRT/M). With γ = 1.40, air at 293 K gives about 343 m/s.
  • Identifying a gas. Measured γ values sort gases by structure: about 1.67 for argon and helium, 1.40 for nitrogen, oxygen and air, and about 1.3 for water vapour and methane.
  • Heat capacities in labs. A mole of diatomic gas needs 20.8 J to warm by 1 K at constant volume, against 12.5 J for a monatomic one.
09

Summary

In one line. Equipartition gives every quadratic mode ½ kT per molecule, and the chain f → CV → CP → γ turns a count of modes into the numbers measured for a gas.

Key points

  • f = 3, 5 and 6 for monatomic, diatomic and non-linear polyatomic molecules, with vibration frozen.
  • CV = (f/2)R, CP = CV + R and γ = 1 + 2/f.
  • U = nCVT depends on T; the mode count does not, within the sim's range.

Common mix-ups

  • "Each gas has its own γ that has to be looked up." Gases with the same molecule type share f, so they share γ. Helium, neon and argon all give 5/3.
  • "A dumbbell spins about three axes." The sim counts the two axes at right angles to the bond. Spinning along the bond stores no energy.
  • "More ways to store energy should give a larger γ." CP − CV stays R, so a larger CV makes the ratio smaller.

Things to try on your own

  • At 300 K, subtract U for the monatomic molecule from U for the diatomic one, and compare the difference with R × 300 K.
  • Find the temperature at which the monatomic gas has the same U as the diatomic gas at 300 K.
  • For the polyatomic molecule, divide the CP card by the CV card and compare with 1 + 2/f.
